title: ‘Reaching 50 is a success story’: how one trans woman survived HIV and stigma in Latin America

paragraphs.en: Erika Castellanos has outlived what she describes as one of the cruellest statistics in Latin America. The life expectancy of a transgender woman in the region is estimated to be 35 years. “I am 50 years old. A lot of trans women are killed very early in life, either because of HIV or because of transphobia, so reaching 50 is a success story,” she says.
paragraphs.zh: 埃里卡·卡斯特利亚诺斯（Erika Castellanos）活得比拉丁美洲最残酷的数据之一更久。该地区跨性别女性的预期寿命估计为35岁。“我已经50岁了。很多跨性别女性在很年轻时就被杀害，或是因为艾滋病毒，或是因为跨性别恐惧症，所以活到50岁就是一个成功的故事，”她说。

paragraphs.en: When Castellanos was diagnosed with HIV in 1995, doctors gave her six months to live. She had already spent years watching Aids devastate her community, with effective treatment beyond the reach of most people in low-income countries.
paragraphs.zh: 1995年卡斯特利亚诺斯被诊断感染艾滋病毒时，医生说她只剩下六个月的寿命。此前她已多年目睹艾滋病摧毁她的社区，而有效的治疗对低收入国家的大多数人来说遥不可及。

paragraphs.en: Looking back over the past 30 years, Castellanos, born and raised in Belize, says the medical breakthrough has been extraordinary. She began treatment in 2000 using whatever medicines arrived as donations to hospitals.
paragraphs.zh: 回顾过去30年，在伯利兹出生并长大的卡斯特利亚诺斯说，医学上的突破是惊人的。2000年，她开始接受治疗，用的是以捐赠形式送到医院的各种药物。

paragraphs.en: “When I was diagnosed, we were taking whatever came our way. Most of it came as donations from Europe and the United States. Science has come such a long way. Every time we’re getting closer to a cure, closer to a vaccine,” she says.
paragraphs.zh: 她说：“我确诊的时候，我们抓到什么药就用什么药。大部分药物来自欧洲和美国的捐赠。科学已经取得了长足的进步。我们每一次都在更接近治愈，更接近疫苗。”

paragraphs.en: After moving from Belize to neighbouring Mexico in the early 1990s to live more openly as a trans woman, she survived through sex work and volunteered at an HIV hospice in southern Mexico.
paragraphs.zh: 上世纪90年代初，她从伯利兹搬到邻国墨西哥，希望作为跨性别女性更公开地生活。她靠性工作维持生计，并在墨西哥南部的一家艾滋病临终关怀院做志愿者。

paragraphs.en: “We barely had anything [at the hospice]. My mother paid for the snacks at our meetings. It was a time when treatment options were extremely limited. We were caring for people who were dying. We were giving comfort because there wasn’t much else we could do,” she says.
paragraphs.zh: 她说：“（在那家临终关怀院）我们几乎一无所有。我母亲为我们开会时的茶点付钱。那是一个治疗选择极其有限的年代。我们在照顾垂死的人。我们在给予安慰，因为除此之外我们无能为力。”

paragraphs.en: When it came to her own health, Castellanos feared hospitals almost as much as she feared HIV, never knowing whether healthcare workers would treat her with dignity or humiliation.
paragraphs.zh: 至于她自己的健康，卡斯特利亚诺斯对医院的恐惧几乎不亚于对艾滋病毒的恐惧，她永远不知道医护人员会以尊严还是羞辱对待她。

paragraphs.en: “There was a lot of stigma at the time. [Hospital staff] would tell me, ‘You have HIV because you chose this life,’ but I don’t have HIV because I chose anything; I have HIV because there was no system that allowed me to protect myself. I was forced into situations that carried risks. Nobody would ever choose this,” she says.
paragraphs.zh: 她说：“当时有很多污名。（医院工作人员）会告诉我，‘你感染艾滋是因为你选择了这种生活’，但我感染艾滋并不是因为我选择了什么；我感染艾滋是因为没有任何制度允许我保护自己。我被逼进了充满风险的情境。没有人会自愿选择这种生活。”
